newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer stiffens verbal intervention on mark.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer stiffens verbal intervention on mark.

text.p: The Bundesbank sought on Thursday to cool currency-market speculation against the mark, but financial analysts said more weakness was likely if the German authorities go no further than verbal intervention.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he was watching developments "very carefully" and hoped the mark's correction against the dollar did not go too far.

"For the most part exchange rate developments are the result of corrections which were necessary. I hope now that it will not come to an overreaction," Tietmeyer told Spanish journalists in Frankfurt.

Tietmeyer's comments followed a statement on Wednesday by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet saying that Germany was in touch with its partners on the mark. The German unit rebounded slightly from Tuesday's six year low below 1.80 to the dollar.

But currency strategists said the mild tone of comments by both Bonn and Frankfurt this week showed Germany was prepared to live with a weaker mark and that action in the form of currency intervention or interest rate hikes was not imminent.

"We think that neither should be feared at current forex rates because nobody really resents this development -- rather it is welcome," Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt, said.

Currency strategists expect to hear more of the same when Kohl holds his traditional summer news conference on Friday -- his last appearance before the Bonn press before his summer vacation in the Austrian Alps.
They say Kohl is likely to repeat typical statements made by German leaders recently -- that the euro will be as strong as the mark, and that EMU will start on time.
Government sources, loath to upset forex markets, told Reuters the current weakness of the mark increased the need to ensure the euro is a solid currency.
The sources also said worries that the euro might be weak were causing an overreaction on forex markets as investors shift funds into "Anglo-Saxon" currencies.

But, the analysts said, official statements do little to hide the fact that the sputtering German economy -- hit by record post-war unemployment and slack domestic demand -- is unable to sustain the mark's traditional strength.

"The German economy cannot live with a strong mark," Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Citibank in London, said. "Recovery to date has been exclusively dependent on exports -- largely courtesy of the weak mark over the past two years."
Analysts said they saw no chance of the Bundesbank raising interest rates if the mark steadies near current levels. A rapid fall to around 1.90 would, however, force a rate hike.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp, in comments published on Thursday, also played down recent currency market action as "unspectacular", saying the mark correction was over.
In an interview, held on Tuesday with Wirtschaftswoche magazine, Krupp also said that the Bundesbank's monetary policy could not be used to steer foreign exchange markets.
"It was always the declared policy of the Bundesbank, that monetary policy in an anchor currency country cannot be used to exercise exchange rate policy and to influence exchange rates," Krupp said.

Krupp declined direct comment on the likely outcome of the Bundesbank's next council meeting next Thursday. "But one must see rationally; the domestic economy does not at present give any reason to alter interest rates," he said.

Some currency strategists said that Bonn and Frankfurt's passive position could encourage more dollar buying in a market which still likes the greenback thanks to its higher yield, its status as a save haven from EMU, and the strong U.S. economy.

"It does indicate that Germany is not committed to maintaining a strong mark," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago. "The Bundesbank may not like a weak mark, but there is little they can do about it at the moment."

Citibank's MacKinnon agreed: "Investors are happy to push the dollar up to the 1.80 level, but increasingly currency economists and investors feel there is little impediment at this level. The market is talking about 1.90 or even two."
